headline: Americans feel a little better as gas prices fall

sources.title: US Consumer Confidence Increased in October (The Conference Board)
US consumer confidence recovers in October as gas prices eased a bit (AP, via ABC News)
Consumer confidence edges up on decline in gas prices: Conference Board (CFO Dive)

chunks.text: Americans felt a little better about the economy in October 2026, as gas got a bit cheaper. The news {{came out}} on October 27 from The Conference Board, a [[nonprofit]] [[research group]]. Every month, some Americans {{fill out}} its [[online survey]] about jobs, business and money. Their answers become the [[consumer confidence index]], a score that shows how good people feel about the economy.

verbs.why: Test results come out a week after the exam. The jobs report comes out every month. The news came out on October 27 from The Conference Board.

verbs.correct: To complete a form or survey
verbs.wrong: To write the questions for a survey
verbs.why: Patients fill out a short form at the doctor's office. Many students fill out job applications in the spring. Every month, some Americans fill out The Conference Board's online survey.

chunks.text: In October, the index {{bounced back}} by 7.5 points to 91.7, its highest level since June 2026. In September, it was 84.2, the lowest since April 2014. People also felt more hopeful when they {{looked ahead}} six months. A [[senior economist]] at the group said the [[recovery]] matched the drop in gas prices from September to October.

verbs.correct: To rise again after a fall
verbs.wrong: To change many times in a row
verbs.why: Sales often bounce back after a slow month. The stock market usually bounces back after a bad day. In October, the consumer confidence index bounced back by 7.5 points to 91.7.
Many people look ahead and save money for later. Smart travelers look ahead and plan their trips early. People felt more hopeful when they looked ahead six months.

chunks.text: According to a large club for drivers that tracks gas prices, a [[gallon]] of regular gas cost $4.27 [[on average]] on October 27. A month earlier, it cost $4.48. So prices {{went down}} by 21 cents, which helps drivers who {{fill up}} their tanks. But a year earlier, a gallon cost only $3.05. The economist {{pointed out}} that confidence is still on a long [[downward trend]]. Many people in the survey were still [[frustrated]] by rising costs. [[Worries]] about jobs also {{showed up}} a bit more often.

verbs.wrong: To be shown on a sign
verbs.why: Hotel prices go down after the summer. Fruit prices often go down when the weather is good. Gas prices went down by 21 cents from September to October.

verbs.correct: To fill a car's gas tank completely
verbs.wrong: To check the air in the tires
verbs.why: My dad fills up the car every Friday. Many drivers fill up at the same gas station each week. Lower gas prices help drivers who fill up their tanks.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.why: My friend points out that the store closes early on Sundays. Doctors often point out the risks of a new drug. The economist pointed out that confidence is still on a long downward trend.

verbs.wrong: To be solved by the bank
verbs.why: Spelling mistakes show up in many emails. New words show up in the dictionary every year. Worries about jobs showed up a bit more often in the survey comments.

chunks.text: [[Inflation]], the general rise in prices, is still a problem. The U.S. Labor Department reports that consumer prices {{went up}} 3.7 percent in September from a year earlier. The economist said high prices have {{eaten into}} people's [[buying power]]. Over the next six months, people plan to {{cut back}} on [[services]], such as hotels and air travel. They also plan to spend less on [[big purchases]] like phones. Plans for movies, concerts and sports games {{held up}} better. And {{eating out}} is at the top of their [[spending plans]] for services.

verbs.why: Rent goes up in many cities each year. Bus fares go up when fuel costs more. Consumer prices went up 3.7 percent in September from a year earlier.

verbs.correct: To reduce something bit by bit
verbs.wrong: To split something in two equal parts
verbs.why: Car repairs eat into the money we save for vacation. Long meetings eat into my time for real work. The economist said high prices have eaten into people's buying power.
Students cut back on coffee to save money. We cut back on gifts when bills are high. Over the next six months, people plan to cut back on services, such as hotels and air travel.

verbs.correct: To stay strong and not fall
verbs.why: Ticket sales hold up well in a slow economy. Some small shops hold up better than big stores in hard times. Plans for movies, concerts and sports games held up better.
We eat out on Friday nights. Many young people eat out two or three times a week. Eating out is at the top of people's spending plans for services.

mainIdea.s: Americans felt more hopeful about the economy in October, mostly because gas got a little cheaper. Still, an expert says confidence stays weak over the long run as prices remain high.
mainIdea.why: The consumer confidence index bounced back as gas prices went down. But the economist pointed out that confidence is still on a long downward trend.

mainIdea.s: Cheaper gas lifted Americans' mood about money in October after a very weak September. An expert says the long slide in confidence is over and spending should rise again soon.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the economist pointed out that confidence is still on a long downward trend, and people still plan to cut back.

mainIdea.s: Gas stations across the country will lower prices next month after a new law takes effect. Drivers in several states are already making plans for longer road trips this winter.
mainIdea.why: A monthly survey shows how Americans feel about the economy. Confidence bounced back in October as gas prices went down.

tf.s: Americans felt better about the economy as gas prices went down.
tf.why: Gas prices went down from September to October, and the consumer confidence index rose by 7.5 points.

tf.s: The consumer confidence index fell again in October.
tf.why: The index bounced back in October after a very low score in September.

tf.s: Many people in the survey were still frustrated by rising costs.
tf.why: Their comments still talked about high prices, and worries about jobs also showed up more often.

tf.s: The economist said confidence is now on a strong upward trend.
tf.why: He pointed out that confidence is still on a long downward trend.

tf.s: People plan to spend more on big purchases like phones.
tf.why: They plan to cut back on services and to spend less on big purchases over the next six months.

tf.s: Gas is still more expensive than it was a year ago.
tf.why: Drivers who fill up pay $4.27 a gallon on average, compared with $3.05 a year earlier.

lines.text: Did you see the news about consumer confidence?
Every month, people {{fill out}} a survey about jobs, business and money. The answers become a score for how good people feel about the economy.
And how do people feel right now?
A little better. The score {{bounced back}} in October, after a really bad September.
[[That's more like it]]. Why the change?
Mostly gas. Prices {{went down}} by about twenty cents a gallon.
That [[sounds about right]]. It was cheaper when I {{filled up}} on Sunday.
Twenty cents isn't much, but it gives families a little [[wiggle room]].
Still, gas costs way more than it did last year.
Right. A gallon was about three dollars then. And an economist {{pointed out}} that confidence is still on a long downward trend.
So the good news is [[nothing to write home about]].
Not really. Prices {{went up}} 3.7 percent in September, and that {{eats into}} everyone's paycheck.
They plan to {{cut back}} on services and on things like new phones and laptops.
But I bet people still {{eat out}}.
They do. Restaurants are at the top of their spending plans.
Well, I'm a [[glass half full]] person. Cheaper gas is a good start.

expressions.def: Used to say that things are now better, the way you wanted

expressions.def: Used to say that something seems correct to you

expressions.def: A little extra money, time or space that lets you change your plans
ex: A small raise gives us some wiggle room each month.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is just OK and not special
ex: The hotel was clean, but it was nothing to write home about.

expressions.def: Used to describe a person who sees the good side of things
ex: My sister is a glass half full person, even on bad days.
